reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / DeVita's Cancer: Principles & Practice of Oncology
clinicalPearls: The great majority are squamous cell carcinomas strongly linked to persistent high-risk human papillomavirus infection, particularly HPV types 16 and 18
Risk is increased in people with a history of receptive anal intercourse, multiple sexual partners, HIV infection, immunosuppression, and prior HPV-related anogenital neoplasia
Common presenting features include anal bleeding, a palpable lump, discomfort or pain, pruritus, and a sensation of a mass, which are frequently misattributed to haemorrhoids
Digital rectal examination and inguinal node assessment are essential, and any persistent or atypical anal lesion should be biopsied rather than assumed benign
The cornerstone of curative treatment is combined chemoradiotherapy, which preserves the anal sphincter and avoids the need for a permanent stoma in most patients
Surgery in the form of abdominoperineal resection is generally reserved for residual or recurrent disease after chemoradiotherapy rather than as first-line therapy
Anal squamous cell cancer must be distinguished from rectal adenocarcinoma extending to the anus, as their management pathways differ substantially
Screening and surveillance with anal cytology and high-resolution anoscopy are considered for high-risk groups such as people living with HIV
reference.pathophysiology: Most anal cancers develop from squamous or transitional epithelium of the anal canal, driven by persistent infection with oncogenic human papillomavirus. Viral oncoproteins inactivate tumour suppressor pathways, producing progressive squamous intraepithelial lesions (anal intraepithelial neoplasia) that can advance to invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Immunosuppression, especially from HIV, impairs viral clearance and accelerates this process. Tumours spread locally into the sphincter complex and surrounding tissues and metastasise to inguinal, perirectal, and pelvic lymph nodes.
additionalDifferentials: Rectal adenocarcinoma extending to the anal canal
Anal melanoma or other rare anal tumours
additionalInvestigations: Digital rectal examination with inspection and palpation of inguinal nodes
Biopsy of the anal lesion for histological confirmation
Pelvic MRI to assess local tumour extent and nodal involvement
CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis, and PET-CT where available, for staging
HIV testing and assessment of immune status given the strong association
redFlags: Persistent anal bleeding or a non-healing anal lesion attributed to haemorrhoids
A firm or ulcerated anal mass with associated pain
Enlarged inguinal lymph nodes suggesting nodal spread
New anal symptoms in an immunosuppressed or HIV-positive patient
reference.prognosis: Localised anal squamous cell carcinoma has a favourable prognosis with organ-preserving chemoradiotherapy and high rates of local control; outcome worsens with larger tumours, nodal involvement, and metastatic disease.
pitfalls: Diagnosing haemorrhoids without examining or biopsying a persistent anal lesion
Confusing anal squamous cell carcinoma with rectal adenocarcinoma and applying the wrong treatment pathway
Proceeding to primary radical surgery instead of first-line chemoradiotherapy
Overlooking HIV status and immunosuppression that influence management and prognosis
references: DeVita's Cancer: Principles & Practice of Oncology
management: Definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy with a fluoropyrimidine plus mitomycin is the curative standard for localized squamous cell carcinoma, preserving the anal sphincter; a cisplatin-based regimen is an alternative with similar efficacy
Radiotherapy is delivered by IMRT rather than older techniques to reduce skin, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary toxicity
Radiotherapy alone can be considered for frail or elderly patients with early, low-risk disease who cannot tolerate chemotherapy, but chemoradiotherapy is preferred when tolerated

A narrow subset of small, well-differentiated, superficial perianal lesions without sphincter or nodal involvement may be managed with local excision alone, reserving chemoradiotherapy for close/positive margins or higher-risk features

Tumor regression after chemoradiotherapy can continue for up to a year, so repeat biopsy of a slowly regressing lesion should generally be avoided; only clearly progressive or non-regressing/recurrent disease should be biopsied

Confirmed persistent or recurrent disease after chemoradiotherapy is managed with salvage abdominoperineal resection, adding groin dissection for involved inguinal nodes and en bloc resection for adjacent organ invasion; negative margins are the strongest predictor of survival
Tissue flap reconstruction is frequently used after salvage APR given the high rate of perineal wound complications

Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma is treated with systemic chemotherapy, preferring a platinum-taxane combination as first-line, with platinum-fluoropyrimidine as an alternative and a docetaxel-platinum-fluoropyrimidine triplet as another option
Metastasectomy can be considered for carefully selected patients with limited metastatic disease, particularly isolated liver metastases, and good performance status
PD-1-targeted checkpoint inhibitor monotherapy is a second-line option for refractory, unresectable, or metastatic disease
Chemoradiotherapy should generally not be withheld in HIV-positive patients, though low CD4 counts warrant closer toxicity monitoring during treatment
Any persistent or atypical anal lesion, or bleeding misattributed to hemorrhoids, warrants biopsy and referral rather than empirical treatment for benign anorectal disease
New diagnoses should be managed within a multidisciplinary team spanning radiation oncology, medical oncology, and colorectal/surgical oncology

Post-treatment surveillance relies on clinical examination, anoscopy, and inguinal node palpation starting roughly 8 to 12 weeks after chemoradiotherapy, continuing regularly for several years since most relapses occur within the first three years
